valueChain.summary: Telecom operators pay large fixed sums up front for spectrum and networks, then earn recurring monthly fees from subscribers, so profit depends on spreading those fixed costs over many paying users at a decent ARPU. Infrastructure owners (towers, fibre) earn steady rents by sharing the same assets across several operators.

stages.name: Spectrum and licences
activities: Bid for spectrum in government auctions
Pay licence fees and spectrum charges
Meet roll-out, security and subscriber KYC rules
revenueDrivers: None directly: spectrum is an input that sets coverage and capacity
Better bands (sub-GHz for coverage, mid-band for 5G capacity) support higher ARPU and lower churn
costDrivers: Auction price per MHz and amount of spectrum bought
Licence fee as a share of revenue (8% of AGR in India)

kpis.name: Licence fee and SUC as % of AGR
kpis.formula: (licence fee + spectrum usage charges) / adjusted gross revenue
kpis.benchmark: Licence fee 8% of AGR (3% licence plus 5% Digital Bharat Nidhi). No SUC on spectrum bought in auctions since 2022, but older spectrum still pays, so SUC is now about 1-1.5% of industry AGR (approx., 2025)

kpis.name: Spectrum held per licence area
kpis.formula: MHz held across all bands in a circle
kpis.benchmark: Leading Indian operators hold well over 100 MHz in major circles once 5G mid-band is included (approx.)

stages.marginNote: A cost stage, not a profit stage: the state captures value through auction prices and revenue-linked fees, with the licence fee alone taking about 8% of revenue.

stages.name: Passive infrastructure
activities: Build and lease towers, poles and in-building systems
Lay and lease fibre for backhaul
Supply site power: grid, diesel generators, batteries, solar
revenueDrivers: Rent per tenant per tower or per fibre km
Number of tenants sharing each asset (tenancy)
Energy pass-through and loading charges for extra equipment
costDrivers: Energy, especially diesel at sites with poor grid supply

kpis.name: Tenancy ratio
kpis.benchmark: About 1.6x for India's largest tower company (approx., 2025-26); above 2x is strong by global standards

kpis.name: Fibre-connected towers
kpis.formula: towers with fibre backhaul / total towers
kpis.benchmark: Roughly 35-40% of towers in India vs 70-80% in advanced markets (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Attractive: large tower companies earn roughly 50-55% EBITDA on long contracts, and each extra tenant on an existing tower adds revenue at little cost (approx.).

stages.name: Active network and operations
activities: Deploy radios, core network and transmission equipment
Plan coverage and capacity; run the network operations centre
Run IT systems (OSS/BSS) that provision and meter services
revenueDrivers: Coverage and speed that let the operator charge more and lose fewer users
Spare capacity sold as fixed wireless broadband or wholesale to MVNOs
costDrivers: Radio and core capex per site
Network operations staff and outsourced O&M

kpis.name: Network availability
kpis.formula: time network is up / total time

kpis.name: Data usage per subscriber
kpis.benchmark: About 30-45 GB a month for leading Indian operators (approx., 2026)

stages.marginNote: Operators earn high EBITDA (roughly 40-60% for Indian operators) but heavy network capex keeps return on capital low; equipment vendors run on thinner operating margins of roughly 5-15% (approx.).

stages.name: Products, pricing and content
activities: Design prepaid packs and postpaid plans
Bundle OTT content, devices and home broadband
Set wholesale terms for MVNOs and enterprise products
revenueDrivers: Tariff per pack and the mix of packs users choose
Share of postpaid and converged (mobile plus broadband) customers
Add-ons: data top-ups, roaming, OTT bundles
costDrivers: Content fees for OTT services bundled into plans

kpis.name: ARPU
kpis.benchmark: About ₹175-265 for Indian private operators (approx., mid-2026)

kpis.name: Postpaid share of base
kpis.benchmark: Under 10% in India vs well over half in many developed markets (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Where the operator captures value: a ₹10 tariff rise on 30 crore subscribers adds about ₹3,600 crore of revenue a year with almost no extra cost beyond revenue-linked levies and commissions.

stages.name: Distribution and acquisition
activities: Sell SIMs, complete KYC and activate
Run the recharge network: retailers, apps, wallets
Win port-ins from rivals through number portability
revenueDrivers: Recharge value flowing through each channel
costDrivers: Commissions on recharges and new SIMs
SIM and KYC cost per activation

kpis.name: Cost per gross add
kpis.benchmark: A few hundred rupees per prepaid gross add in India (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Thin for intermediaries: distributors and retailers keep a few per cent of recharge value, and digital recharge is cheaper for the operator than retail.

stages.name: Customer care, billing and retention
activities: Bill and collect postpaid; manage prepaid balances
Predict churn and make retention offers
revenueDrivers: Upsell and plan migration during customer contacts

kpis.name: Monthly churn
kpis.formula: subscribers lost in month / opening subscribers
kpis.benchmark: About 2-3% for Indian prepaid, around 1% or less for postpaid (approx.)

kpis.name: First-contact resolution
kpis.formula: issues solved on first contact / total issues

stages.marginNote: A cost centre (a few per cent of revenue) that protects revenue: one point of monthly churn on a 30 crore base is 30 lakh subscribers lost every month.

valueChain.profitPools: In absolute terms most EBITDA sits with operators, which earn roughly 40-60% EBITDA margins in India, but spectrum (s1) and network capex (s3) absorb much of it, so their returns on capital are modest. Passive infrastructure (s2) earns the best risk-adjusted returns, because long contracts and extra tenants on existing towers or fibre add revenue at little cost. The state captures a large share up front through auctions and revenue-linked fees, while distribution (s5) and care (s6) are thin-margin service businesses for the firms that run them.

unitEconomics.unit: per mobile subscriber per month (large Indian operator, simplified, approx.)

lines.item: Licence fee and spectrum usage charges (~9% of revenue)
Network opex: tower rent, energy, maintenance

unitEconomics.result: Pre-tax profit ≈ ₹45 per subscriber per month (EBITDA ≈ ₹112, about 51% of ARPU)

valueChain.india: India has about 115 crore mobile subscribers (excluding machine-to-machine connections), served almost entirely by three private operators and state-owned BSNL/MTNL after a decade of consolidation; over 90% are prepaid and ARPU is among the lowest in the world. The Department of Telecommunications auctions spectrum and charges an 8% licence fee on adjusted gross revenue (AGR), TRAI oversees tariffs and interconnection, and the 2019 Supreme Court ruling on AGR dues showed how far regulation can reshape the industry. Towers and fibre are widely shared through independent tower companies, and 5G has been rolling out since October 2022.

workedExample.problem: An Indian operator's EBITDA margin fell 3 points (50% to 47%) in a year even though ARPU rose 5%.
trace: Revenue is up 5% (index 100 to 105), so the cause is on the cost side: costs rose from 50 to about 55.7, or 11%.
Revenue-linked costs move with revenue: licence fee and SUC (s1) went from 9 to 9.45 and commissions (s5) from 4 to 4.2, so they leave the margin unchanged.
Care, IT and overheads (s6 and corporate) grew only about 3%, from 15 to 15.4.
That leaves network opex (s2 and s3): it rose from 22 to about 26.6, up 21%, taking it from 22% to 25% of revenue.
Inside network opex, new 5G radios lifted power load at sites in low-traffic areas, many reliant on diesel, so energy and rent grew well ahead of the traffic and revenue they carry.
workedExample.lesson: Revenue-linked costs rarely explain a margin change; look for fixed costs, usually network, that grew ahead of revenue.

cases.title: Circle EBITDA decline at mobile operator
cases.prompt: Our client is a mid-sized Indian mobile operator. In one Category B telecom circle its EBITDA fell from ₹1,600 crore to ₹1,350 crore over two years, even though its subscriber base stayed flat at about 2.5 crore. Why have profits fallen, and what should it do?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Is the fall driven by revenue or costs? A: Both. Revenue fell from ₹4,500 crore to ₹4,350 crore and operating costs rose from ₹2,900 crore to ₹3,000 crore.

Q: What happened to subscribers and ARPU? A: Subscribers were flat at about 2.5 crore, but mobile ARPU fell from ₹140 to ₹135 a month. Other revenue (enterprise, roaming) was flat at about ₹300 crore.

Q: What is happening in the market? A: The two larger rivals rolled out 5G across the circle's towns last year; the client's 5G covers only the circle capital. Many users carry two SIMs, and a growing share keep the client's SIM on its cheapest validity pack.
Q: Which costs rose? A: Mainly network costs, after the client added 4G capacity sites and started 5G; licence fees fell slightly in line with revenue.

modelTree.label: Why did circle EBITDA fall from ₹1,600 crore to ₹1,350 crore?

children.label: Revenue fell ₹150 crore (₹4,500 crore to ₹4,350 crore)
Mix: more users on minimum validity packs
Price: tariffs and discounts per pack
Other revenue (enterprise, roaming): flat at ₹300 crore
Operating costs rose ₹100 crore (₹2,900 crore to ₹3,000 crore)
Network opex: tower rent, energy, maintenance
Licence fee and spectrum usage charges
Interconnect, customer care, IT and staff

hypotheses: Users are making a rival with wider 5G their primary SIM and keeping the client's SIM on the cheapest validity pack, which cut ARPU from ₹140 to ₹135.
Network opex rose by most of the ₹100 crore cost increase because new capacity and 5G sites were added before traffic grew.
hints: Use the profit equation, then check which side explains more of the ₹250 crore fall.
First-level branches: revenue and operating costs.
Operating costs: network opex, licence fee and spectrum charges, distribution commissions, then interconnect, care, IT and staff.

keyMetrics.name: ARPU
keyMetrics.formula: mobile service revenue / average subscribers / 12

keyMetrics.name: EBITDA margin
keyMetrics.formula: EBITDA / revenue (35.6% two years ago, 31.0% now)

commonMistakes: Concluding that subscribers are fine because the count is flat, without asking whether the client has become the secondary SIM on minimum recharges.
Going straight to cost cutting, when revenue fell ₹150 crore and costs rose only ₹100 crore, so revenue explains the larger part.

frameworkPick.why: The question is why EBITDA fell, which is answered by splitting profit into revenue and cost drivers and finding which moved.

distractorWhyNot.growth: The client is not asking how to grow; it needs to diagnose a profit fall first.
distractorWhyNot.competitive-response: Rivals' 5G may be a cause, but the question asks for the cause of the profit fall, not how to react to a specific competitor move.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Operations covers only the cost side and would miss the larger fall in revenue.

cases.title: Size India's home broadband market
cases.prompt: Our client, a large Indian cable TV operator, is thinking of upgrading its network to sell home broadband. As a first step it wants a sense of scale. How big is India's home fixed broadband market today, in annual revenue?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What counts as fixed broadband? A: Home connections over fibre, cable or DSL, plus 5G fixed wireless. Exclude mobile hotspots and business connections.
Q: How many households are there? A: Assume about 31 crore: 4 crore in metros and Tier 1 cities, 7 crore in smaller towns and 20 crore in villages.
Q: What share have broadband? A: Assume about 50% of metro and Tier 1 homes, 25% of smaller-town homes and 4% of rural homes.
Q: What do they pay? A: Assume about ₹650 a month in metros and Tier 1, ₹500 in smaller towns and ₹400 in villages.

modelTree.label: Annual revenue from home fixed broadband in India (₹ crore)

hypotheses: The market is about ₹30,000 crore a year: roughly 4.5 crore homes at a blended spend of about ₹550 a month.
Metros and Tier 1 cities are only about 13% of households but about 52% of revenue (₹15,600 crore), so the client's entry city mix matters more than its national reach.
hints: Size by segment, because penetration and spend differ hugely across the country.
Three segments: metros and Tier 1 cities, smaller towns, villages.
Villages: ~20 crore households x ~4% with broadband x ~₹400 a month x 12 ≈ ₹3,840 crore.

keyMetrics.name: Segment revenue
keyMetrics.formula: households x broadband penetration x monthly spend x 12

keyMetrics.name: Blended ARPU
keyMetrics.formula: total annual revenue / broadband homes / 12 (≈ ₹550)

commonMistakes: Starting from population (about 145 crore people) instead of households, when broadband is bought per home.
Using one national penetration rate and price, which hides that metros are a small share of homes but about half of revenue.

frameworkPick.why: The question is 'how big', a single number built from households, penetration and spend; no entry decision is being asked yet.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: Entry is the later decision; this question only asks for the size of the prize.
distractorWhyNot.growth: The client has no broadband business to grow yet.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Segments are used to size more accurately, but the output is a market size, not a choice of target customers.

cases.title: Pricing a family add-on line
cases.prompt: Our client is a mid-sized Spanish mobile operator whose main postpaid plan costs €25 a month. It wants to let account holders add a line for a family member on the same bill. What monthly price should it charge for each extra line?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Raise lines per account and cut churn; the target is for 20% of its 2 million postpaid accounts to add at least one line within 18 months.
Q: What does an extra line cost us? A: About €3 a month in network and care costs, plus about €15 one-off for the SIM and activation.
Q: What do competitors charge? A: The two larger operators charge €8-12 a month for add-on lines; low-cost brands sell standalone SIM-only plans from about €7.
Q: Anything on churn? A: Accounts with two or more lines churn about 0.8% a month, against 1.5% for single-line accounts.

modelTree.label: What monthly price should the add-on family line carry?

children.label: Incremental cost: ~€3 a month plus €15 one-off
Cannibalisation: members who would have bought a €25 plan
Churn saving on the whole account (1.5% to 0.8%)
Value of one bill and family controls to the payer
Need by member type: child, partner, elderly parent
Shared data pool vs own allowance per line
Likely rival reaction to our price

hypotheses: A price of about €8-10 clears the €3 cost, matches the low end of rivals and sits close to €7 low-cost SIMs, so families have no reason to keep a member on another brand.
Cutting account churn from 1.5% to 0.8% a month nearly doubles expected account life (about 67 to 125 months), so the line should be priced for take-up rather than for margin on the line itself.
hints: Split by the perspectives that set or bound a price.
Branches: our economics per added line, families' willingness to pay, competitor reference prices.
Competitor references: larger rivals' add-on lines at €8-12, low-cost standalone SIMs from €7, and how rivals would react to our price.

keyMetrics.name: Monthly contribution per add-on line
keyMetrics.formula: add-on price - €3 incremental cost

keyMetrics.name: Expected account life (months)
keyMetrics.formula: 1 / monthly churn

commonMistakes: Pricing off cost alone (€3) or off competitors alone, without valuing the churn saving on the whole €25 account.
Ignoring cannibalisation: a cheap add-on lets families move a member off a full €25 plan.

frameworkPick.why: The product is decided and the question is the price point, which comes from cost, customer value and competitor references.

distractorWhyNot.product-launch: The client has already decided to offer the line; only the price is open.
distractorWhyNot.growth: More lines per account is the aim, but the question asked is a single pricing decision.
distractorWhyNot.competitive-response: No rival has made a move the client must answer; competitor prices are just one input.

cases.title: Doubling postpaid subscribers in three years
cases.prompt: Our client is a large Indian mobile operator with 30 crore subscribers, of which only 2.4 crore (8%) are postpaid. Postpaid ARPU is about 2.5 times prepaid. The CEO wants to double postpaid subscribers to 4.8 crore in three years. How should the client get there?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Where do postpaid customers come from today? A: About 60% of gross adds are the client's own prepaid users migrating, 30% port in from rivals and 10% are brand-new numbers.
Q: How many are we losing? A: Monthly postpaid churn is about 1%, roughly half port-outs and half downgrades to prepaid or non-payment disconnections.
Q: Who could migrate? A: About 4 crore of the client's prepaid users spend over ₹400 a month; surveys say fear of bill shock and credit checks hold them back.
Q: Any constraints? A: Postpaid ARPU is about ₹480 against about ₹190 for prepaid, and the CEO does not want to cut postpaid prices.

modelTree.label: How to grow postpaid from 2.4 crore to 4.8 crore in three years?

children.label: Migrate more of our own prepaid users
Target the ~4 crore prepaid users spending ₹400+
Remove barriers: bill caps, lighter credit checks
Incentives: family add-on lines, bundled OTT
Win more port-ins from rival operators
Rivals' postpaid users: compete on network and service
Rivals' high-spend prepaid users: offer a postpaid switch
Ease switching: doorstep SIM delivery, bill credits
Fewer port-outs: fix network and service pain points
Fewer downgrades to prepaid: right-size plans

hypotheses: Own-prepaid migration is the biggest pool: converting 15% of the 4 crore users spending ₹400+ adds about 60 lakh postpaid subscribers.

At 1% monthly churn on a base growing evenly from 2.4 to 4.8 crore (about 3.6 crore on average), the client loses about 1.3 crore postpaid users over three years, so halving churn is worth about 65 lakh subscribers, over a quarter of the 2.4 crore target.
hints: Use a stock-and-flow bridge for the postpaid base.
Branches: migrate own prepaid users, win port-ins from rivals, add brand-new numbers, lose fewer postpaid subscribers.
Port-ins: rivals' postpaid users (network and service), rivals' high-spend prepaid users (a postpaid switch offer), and easier switching (doorstep SIMs, bill credits).

keyMetrics.name: Postpaid net adds
keyMetrics.formula: own-prepaid migrations + port-ins + brand-new numbers - disconnections

keyMetrics.name: Gross adds needed over three years
keyMetrics.formula: 2.4 crore target + ~1.3 crore expected churn ≈ 3.7 crore

commonMistakes: Looking only at acquisition: with 1% monthly churn the gross-add target is about 3.7 crore, not 2.4 crore.
Listing 'family add-on lines' as a separate source, when each new family line is a migration, a port-in or a new number, which double-counts.

frameworkPick.why: The client wants to grow one customer base to a target, so the tree splits net growth into sources of additions and losses.

distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Targeting high-spend prepaid users helps, but the question is how to reach a growth target, not how to divide the market.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: The CEO has ruled out price cuts, and price is only one lever among several.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: New postpaid offers may be one lever, but the question is how to reach a subscriber target across all sources of additions and losses, not whether to launch a product.

cases.title: Cutting energy cost at rural sites
cases.prompt: Our client is a mid-sized Indian mobile operator that owns and runs 40,000 rural sites. Energy for these sites costs ₹1,300 crore a year, up 25% in two years, and the CFO wants it cut by 20% within 18 months without hurting network availability. How would you do it?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What makes up the spend? A: Grid power supplies about 70% of the energy but only about 45% of the spend; diesel supplies about 30% of the energy but about 55% of the spend. Grid supply averages about 16 hours a day.
Q: Why has it gone up? A: New 5G and extra 4G radios raised average site load from about 2.1 kW to 2.6 kW, and grid tariffs rose slightly.
Q: What are the constraints? A: Network availability must stay above 99.5%, and capex for energy projects is capped at ₹600 crore.
Q: Are any sites shared? A: About 30% host a second operator, which pays its share of energy at a fixed rate per kW agreed five years ago.

modelTree.label: How to cut net rural site energy cost 20% (₹260 crore)?

children.label: Switch off idle 5G and 4G carriers at night
Replace old radios with energy-efficient units
Swap air-conditioned shelters for outdoor cabinets
Free cooling and higher temperature set points
Power conversion and battery charging losses
Pay less per unit of energy
Shift the mix away from diesel (~55% of spend)
Lithium-ion batteries to ride through grid outages
Solar at sites with space and strong sun
Work with DISCOMs to raise grid hours
Correct tariff category and sanctioned load
Audit bills for estimated readings and surcharges
Lower diesel cost per kWh generated
Recover more from tenants on shared sites
Reprice tenant energy charges set five years ago
Move from fixed per-kW rate to actual-cost pass-through
Add tenants to share fixed site energy

hypotheses: Diesel costs about ₹26 per kWh against about ₹9 for grid; halving diesel energy with batteries and solar at the worst-grid sites would save roughly ₹230 crore a year, nearly all of the ₹260 crore target.
The five-year-old fixed per-kW rate under-recovers energy on the 12,000 shared sites, because both load and tariffs have risen since it was set.
Switching off idle carriers at night can cut radio load by 10-15% with no effect on availability, since rural traffic falls sharply after midnight.
hints: Write net energy cost as an equation and split along its terms.
Branches: use less energy per site, pay less per unit of energy, recover more from tenants.
Use less energy: radio load (night carrier switch-off, efficient radios), cooling and shelter load, power conversion and battery losses.

keyMetrics.name: Energy cost per site per month
Cost per kWh by source
keyMetrics.formula: spend on source / kWh from source (diesel ≈ ₹26, grid ≈ ₹9)

keyMetrics.name: Generator run hours per site per day
keyMetrics.formula: total diesel generator hours / sites / days

commonMistakes: Treating energy as one number instead of splitting it into consumption and cost per unit by source, which hides that diesel is 30% of energy but 55% of spend.
Suggesting cuts to backup or switching off sites, which would breach the 99.5% availability constraint.

frameworkPick.why: The task is to cut one defined cost line under an operating constraint, which calls for splitting the cost into its physical and price drivers.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Revenue is not in question; the problem is already narrowed to one cost line.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: Pricing applies only to the tenant-recovery branch, not to the main levers of load and source mix.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: The business is not in crisis; this is a targeted cost programme.

cases.title: Launching 5G fixed wireless in small towns
cases.prompt: Our client is an Indian mobile operator with 5G in about 900 towns. It is considering launching 5G fixed wireless home broadband in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns where fibre is thin, at ₹600 a month, with an indoor unit that costs it about ₹6,000. Should it launch, and if so, how?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Add 30 lakh home broadband customers in three years, with each customer paying back its upfront cost within 24 months.

Q: What does each customer cost and earn? A: The indoor unit costs about ₹6,000 and installation about ₹1,000. After licence fee, care and backhaul, monthly contribution is about ₹400 on the ₹600 plan.
Q: Is there network capacity? A: A fixed wireless home uses about 350 GB a month against about 35 GB for a mobile user. About 60% of 5G sectors in the target towns have spare capacity.
Q: What is the competition? A: Local cable operators sell 40-100 Mbps fibre at ₹400-500 a month, and a rival operator has launched fixed wireless in some of the same towns.

modelTree.label: Should we launch ₹600 5G fixed wireless in Tier 2-3 towns, and how?

children.label: Is there enough demand in target towns?
Homes in 5G coverage without good fibre
Homes able to pay ₹600 a month
Homes per sector before mobile users slow down
Indoor signal quality at target homes
Monthly churn and device recovery on exit
Sequence: towns and sectors with spare capacity first
Channels: mobile retailers, local installers, digital
Device: free with lock-in or refundable deposit

hypotheses: Capacity, not demand, limits the launch: each home loads a cell like about 10 mobile users, so only the ~60% of sectors with headroom can take customers, sector by sector.
Simple payback is about 17.5 months, but a cohort recovers its ₹7,000 within 24 months only if monthly churn stays below about 3%, which is hard against ₹400-500 local cable fibre.
hints: Break the decision into the questions a board would ask before and after saying yes.
Branches: enough demand in target towns, network capacity, customer economics, how to launch.
Demand: addressable homes (in 5G coverage, without good fibre, able to pay ₹600) and the alternatives they already have.

keyMetrics.name: Payback (months)
keyMetrics.formula: (indoor unit + installation) / monthly contribution = ₹7,000 / ₹400 ≈ 17.5

keyMetrics.name: Mobile-equivalent load per home
keyMetrics.formula: fixed wireless GB per month / mobile GB per user ≈ 350 / 35 = 10

commonMistakes: Treating fixed wireless like a mobile plan and ignoring that each home uses about 10 times a mobile user's data, which caps sales per sector.
Comparing ₹600 only with the rival's fixed wireless and missing local cable fibre at ₹400-500, the real alternative in these towns.

frameworkPick.why: The client already operates in these towns and is deciding whether and how to launch a new product on its existing network.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The client already has 5G, customers and distribution in these towns; this is a new product on existing assets, not entry into an unfamiliar market.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: The ₹600 price is given; price is one input to the launch decision, not the question.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Network capacity is one branch, but the question also covers demand, economics and go-to-market.

cases.title: Buying a regional fibre ISP
cases.prompt: Our client is a Brazilian mobile operator with no fixed network. It is considering buying a regional fibre internet provider in the South-East with 600,000 connected homes, for R$2.4 billion or about 8 times EBITDA. The seller stresses three years of 25% subscriber growth. Should the client do the deal? (All figures in this case are illustrative case facts.)
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the strategic aim? A: To sell fibre-plus-mobile bundles in the region. Assume converged customers churn about half as often as mobile-only ones.

Q: What are the target's numbers? A: Assume 600,000 connected homes out of 1.8 million homes passed (33%), ARPU about R$100 a month, revenue about R$720 million and EBITDA about R$300 million. Subscriber growth has slowed from 25% to 8% a year.
Q: How strong is the client in the area? A: Assume about 4 million mobile subscribers in the target's footprint, around 30% of them postpaid.

Q: What does the market look like? A: Fibre is fragmented among many regional providers and the large incumbents. Assume prices fall about 5% a year in competitive cities and recent regional deals were done at 6-9x EBITDA.

modelTree.label: Should the client buy the fibre ISP for R$2.4 billion (8x EBITDA)?

children.label: What is the ISP worth on its own?
Capex to maintain and extend the network
What extra value can we create together?
Sell mobile to the ISP's 600,000 homes
Sell fibre to our 4 million mobile users in footprint
Use ISP fibre for our mobile site backhaul
Is the price right and can we deliver?
R$4,000 per connected home vs cost to build
Keeping local managers and installer teams
Build our own fibre in the footprint
Wholesale access from a neutral fibre network

hypotheses: With growth down to 8% and prices falling 5% a year, the ISP is worth nearer 6-7x EBITDA on its own, so the deal works only if synergies are worth at least R$300-600 million.
Selling fibre to the client's own mobile users is the largest synergy: converting 5% of 4 million users adds about 200,000 homes, a third of the current base.
hints: Use deal-value logic: what the asset is worth to us against what we would pay and what else we could do.
Branches: the ISP's standalone value, synergies together, price and integration risk, alternatives to buying.
Standalone value: revenue outlook (penetration of homes passed, ARPU under price erosion, churn) and margins and capex.

keyMetrics.name: EV / EBITDA
keyMetrics.formula: R$2.4 billion / R$300 million = 8x

keyMetrics.name: Penetration of homes passed
keyMetrics.formula: connected homes / homes passed = 33%

commonMistakes: Paying for bundle synergies that a cheaper wholesale fibre deal could deliver, without testing build or partner options.
Valuing the ISP on its past 25% growth when growth has slowed to 8% and prices are falling.

frameworkPick.why: A strategic buyer is deciding whether a specific acquisition at a specific price creates value: standalone value plus synergies, against price and alternatives.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: Entering fixed broadband is the motive, but the question is about this particular deal and its price.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Growth is the aim, but the decision is a transaction with a price tag.
distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: The buyer is a strategic operator valuing synergies, not a financial investor underwriting a standalone return and exit.

cases.title: Segmenting MSMEs for a business bundle
cases.prompt: Our client, the enterprise arm of a large Indian telecom operator, wants to sell small businesses a bundle of business broadband, mobile lines and simple cloud tools such as GST billing. India has about 6.3 crore MSMEs, over 99% of them micro, but the client has only 2,000 field salespeople. How should it segment the market and decide whom to target first?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the bundle cost? A: Starter bundles are about ₹2,500 a month; larger ones with more lines and cloud seats go up to ₹15,000. Assume an average of about ₹4,000.
Q: Where are the client's assets? A: It has fibre in about 400 towns and about 8 lakh small-business owners already on individual mobile plans.
Q: What is the goal? A: ₹1,000 crore of annual MSME revenue within three years. A field rep closes about three bundles a month.
Q: What is the competition? A: Rival operators sell similar bundles, and local ISPs undercut on broadband alone at ₹500-800 a month.

modelTree.label: Which MSME segments should we target first for a ₹2,500-15,000 bundle?

children.label: How to cut the market into segments
Outside fibre towns (mobile and fixed wireless only)
Number of firms in the segment
Telecom and IT spend per firm per year
Pace of digital adoption (UPI, e-invoicing, cloud)
Fit with our bundle: need for lines plus cloud tools
Our 8 lakh existing small-business mobile users
Field sales vs digital or partner channels
Position vs rival operators and local ISPs

hypotheses: Small enterprises in trade and services inside the 400 fibre towns are the best first target: they need several lines plus broadband and justify a field visit.
Micro sole proprietors are too price-sensitive to justify field reps; they should be served digitally, starting with the 8 lakh already on the client's mobile plans.

The sales force is the binding constraint: ₹1,000 crore needs about 2.1 lakh businesses at ₹4,000 a month, and 2,000 reps at three deals a month close about 2.2 lakh in three years, leaving no room for low-conversion segments.
hints: Structure it as the steps from a market of 6.3 crore firms to a first target list.
Branches: segmentation variables, segment attractiveness, our ability to win.
Segmentation variables: size (micro vs small and medium), sector (trade, services, manufacturing), location vs our fibre towns.

keyMetrics.name: Customers needed
keyMetrics.formula: ₹1,000 crore / (₹4,000 x 12) ≈ 2.1 lakh businesses

keyMetrics.name: Sales capacity over three years
keyMetrics.formula: 2,000 reps x 3 deals a month x 36 months ≈ 2.2 lakh

keyMetrics.name: Segment revenue potential
keyMetrics.formula: firms x annual telecom and IT spend per firm x achievable share

commonMistakes: Segmenting by size alone, when sector and location relative to the fibre network decide whether the bundle fits and can be installed.
Ranking segments by number of firms: 99% of MSMEs are micro, but most cannot or will not pay ₹2,500+ a month.

frameworkPick.why: The client must split a huge, varied customer base and choose where to aim a limited sales force, which is a segment-and-target question.

distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: Segment size is an input, but the output is a choice of targets, not a market estimate.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Revenue growth is the goal, but the question asked is specifically whom to target.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: The bundle is already designed; the open question is which customers to aim it at.

cases.title: Saving a cash-strapped MVNO
cases.prompt: Our client is a German MVNO with 1.2 million subscribers that buys network capacity wholesale from a host operator. It lost €40 million last year and has €30 million of cash left, so at the current burn it runs out in about nine months. How would you turn it around?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the P&L look like? A: ARPU is €12 a month, so revenue is about €173 million. Costs are about €213 million: wholesale fees ~€101 million, customer acquisition ~€42 million, care, billing and IT ~€35 million, other overheads ~€35 million.

Q: How does acquisition work? A: About 600,000 gross adds a year at about €70 each, mostly through price-comparison sites. Monthly churn is 3%, and many customers sit on promotional tariffs from earlier years.
Q: What about the wholesale contract? A: The client pays the host about €7 per subscriber per month with a minimum commitment of 1 million subscribers. The renegotiation window opens in six months.
Q: Who owns it? A: The founder and a minority venture investor, who will fund a bridge only against a credible plan to cash breakeven within 18 months.

modelTree.label: How to close a €40m yearly cash burn within ~9 months' runway?

children.label: Move back-book customers off old promotional tariffs
Sell data add-ons and roaming passes
Targeted retention offers to high-ARPU users
Renegotiate the €7 fee when the window opens
Cut comparison-site spend on high-churn segments
Shift to referrals and own digital channels
Cut agency, office and headcount costs
Venture bridge against a breakeven plan
Sell the base or merge with another MVNO

hypotheses: Each subscriber loses about €2 a month even at steady state: €12 ARPU less €7 wholesale leaves €5, short of about €2.40 care and IT, €2.40 overheads and €2.10 of acquisition cost spread over a 33-month life.
The wholesale renegotiation is the biggest single lever: each €1 off the €7 fee is worth about €14 million a year.
Cutting gross adds to replacement level (about 430,000 a year) saves about €12 million of acquisition cash at once, buying time until the wholesale window opens.
hints: Think in cash, not profit, because the runway decides survival; split along the cash-flow statement.
Branches: raise operating cash inflows, cut operating cash outflows, close the remaining funding gap.
Funding gap: free up working capital (annual plans paid upfront, supplier terms) and raise or replace funding (bridge, sale or merger).

keyMetrics.name: Cash runway (months)
keyMetrics.formula: cash / monthly burn = €30m / (€40m / 12) ≈ 9

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per subscriber per month
keyMetrics.formula: ARPU - wholesale fee - care and IT per subscriber

keyMetrics.name: Customer life (months)
keyMetrics.formula: 1 / monthly churn = 1 / 3% ≈ 33

commonMistakes: Proposing more marketing to grow out of trouble, when each new customer loses money and growth deepens the burn.
Ignoring timing: the wholesale lever lands only after six months, so quick cash moves (acquisition cuts, upfront annual plans, a bridge) must cover the gap until then.

frameworkPick.why: With nine months of cash and losses on every customer, the question is survival plus a path to breakeven, which needs both short-term cash moves and fixes to unit economics.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: A profit diagnosis alone ignores the cash runway and funding moves that decide whether the business survives.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Cost efficiency is one lever, but pricing, churn and funding matter as much.
distractorWhyNot.ma: Selling or merging is one option inside the turnaround, not the whole question.

cases.title: Satellite broadband entry and pricing in India
cases.prompt: Our client is a global low-earth-orbit satellite broadband operator that has just received its Indian authorisation. Assume its consumer kit costs about ₹33,000 to make and its plans elsewhere average the equivalent of ₹4,000 a month. The board sees India's roughly 20 crore rural homes without fixed broadband as a huge opportunity. Should it launch consumer broadband in India, and at what price?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the board want? A: Profitable growth in India within five years; its business case assumes rural homes without broadband are the core market.

Q: What will customers pay? A: Assume a survey of rural homes without broadband shows most would pay ₹300-500 a month. About 1% (roughly 20 lakh homes) would pay ₹2,000 or more, and very few would pay ₹33,000 upfront for a kit.
Q: How many users can we serve? A: Assume engineering estimates the current constellation can serve about 20 lakh Indian users at good speeds; capacity is per beam, so dense clusters fill first.

Q: What are the rules? A: Satellite spectrum is assigned administratively, not auctioned, for a fixed term. Assume an annual spectrum charge of 5% of revenue (the government has been finalising 4-5%) on top of the 8% licence fee, so about 13% in all. Security conditions require Indian gateways and data kept in India; assume about ₹1,500 crore upfront, and clearance can take a year or more.

modelTree.label: Should we launch consumer satellite broadband in India, and at what price?

children.label: Who will buy, and at what price?
Homes with no fibre or 5G option: mass income
Homes with no fibre or 5G option: high income (~20 lakh)
Would pay ₹2,000+ a month (farmhouses, homestays, estates)
Willingness to buy the kit upfront or on EMI
Homes already offered fibre or 5G fixed wireless
Might buy only as a backup for reliability
Beams over dense clusters fill first
Price needed to ration scarce capacity
₹33,000 kit: paid by user or subsidised by us
Installation and support in remote areas
Kit payback at ₹500 vs ₹2,500 a month
What do rules and rivals allow?
Indian gateways and data storage (~₹1,500 crore)
Fibre and 5G fixed wireless spreading into towns
Other satellite entrants, some partnered with telcos
How should we enter and price?
Premium: ₹2,000-3,000 a month for high-income homes
Partner with an Indian telco for reach and service

hypotheses: The 20 crore headline is not the market: at ₹500 a month, after about 13% of revenue-linked levies, a ₹33,000 kit takes about 76 months to pay back, so the mass rural segment is out of reach without a deep subsidy.

Capacity, not demand, binds at the premium end: about 20 lakh homes would pay ₹2,000+, roughly the constellation's 20 lakh-user ceiling, so the client should price high (₹2,000-3,000) and ration capacity; at ₹2,500 the kit pays back in about 15 months.
A telco partner gives faster reach and installation in remote areas than building a direct dealer network from scratch during a year-long clearance.
hints: Combine an entry lens with a pricing lens, letting willingness to pay and capacity drive both.
Branches: who will buy and at what price, can we serve them profitably, what rules and rivals allow, how to enter and price.
Rules and rivals: revenue-linked spectrum and licence charges, Indian gateways and security clearance, then fibre, fixed wireless, BharatNet and other satellite entrants.

keyMetrics.name: Kit payback (months)
keyMetrics.formula: kit cost borne by us / (monthly price x (1 - 13% levies))

keyMetrics.name: Capacity-limited revenue
keyMetrics.formula: users served (max ~20 lakh) x monthly price x 12 (≈ ₹6,000 crore a year at ₹2,500)

commonMistakes: Taking the 20 crore unconnected homes as the market without testing willingness and ability to pay against a ₹33,000 kit.
Pricing for volume when capacity caps users at about 20 lakh, which fills the network with low-value users and leaves premium demand unserved.

frameworkPick.why: The client must decide whether to enter a new country under new rules and rivals, and the entry case turns on the price point, so both lenses are needed.

distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: Sizing is an input, but the question is a go/no-go decision and a price, not 'how big'.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: The client is new to India and faces licensing, local rivals and set-up costs, so this is entry into a new market rather than a new product in an existing one.

cases.title: PE stake in a fibre company
cases.prompt: A private equity fund is considering buying 49% of an Indian fibre infrastructure company that leases about 1.2 lakh route km of fibre, mostly for mobile tower backhaul. EBITDA is about ₹1,100 crore and the seller is asking for an enterprise value of ₹14,000 crore. The fund's thesis is that 5G will push far more towers onto fibre. Should it invest?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What are the financials? A: Revenue is about ₹1,450 crore and EBITDA about ₹1,100 crore (76% margin). Tenancy is 1.15 operators per route km.

Q: Who are the customers? A: The former parent, a mobile operator, provides 85% of revenue under a 20-year master agreement with 2% annual escalators. In year 5, two years from now, the fee per km resets to a benchmark rate about 25% below today's fee.

Q: What is the growth plan? A: The seller's plan assumes tenancy rises to 1.6x in five years. Over the last three years it moved from 1.08x to 1.15x, and the two largest operators mostly build their own fibre on dense routes.
Q: What are the deal terms? A: The fund would hold 49% alongside the former parent, and expects to exit in 5-7 years through an InvIT listing or a sale.

modelTree.label: Should the fund buy 49% of the fibre company at ₹14,000 crore EV?

children.label: Will demand for leased fibre grow?
Share of towers on fibre today vs 5G needs
Largest operators' self-build vs lease choices
Home broadband ISPs extending fibre to homes
Data centres and enterprise long-haul links
Rival fibre networks on the same routes
Lease price trend per route km
85% of revenue from one anchor operator
Year-5 fee reset about 25% below today
Fibre cuts, repair times and SLA penalties
Right-of-way and maintenance cost per km
Can we create value beyond the base case?
Second operators on rural and highway routes
ISP and data-centre tenants on existing routes
Faster repairs to cut SLA penalties
Do price, structure and exit work?
12.7x EBITDA vs listed tower and fibre peers
Returns under base and downside tenancy cases
Minority rights at 49% beside the anchor
Anchor guarantees on volumes and reset terms
Sale to an infrastructure fund or strategic buyer

hypotheses: The year-5 reset cuts revenue by about 21% (roughly ₹300 crore) and, with mostly fixed costs, EBITDA to about ₹790 crore, so the true entry multiple is nearer 18x than 12.7x.
Tenancy will not reach 1.6x: it rose only 0.07x in three years and the largest operators self-build on dense routes, so 1.25-1.3x is a more realistic case.
Any upside lies in non-telco tenants (ISPs, data centres) and rural or highway routes where operators lack their own fibre.
hints: Use the due diligence lens a fund's investment committee would apply.
Branches: will demand grow, how secure is today's business, can we create value, do price, structure and exit work.
Demand: operators' backhaul needs (towers on fibre, self-build vs lease), other buyers (ISPs, data centres), competing supply and lease prices.

keyMetrics.name: Tenancy ratio
keyMetrics.formula: tenant-km leased / route km

keyMetrics.name: EV / EBITDA
keyMetrics.formula: ₹14,000 crore / ₹1,100 crore ≈ 12.7x (≈ 18x on post-reset EBITDA of ~₹790 crore)

keyMetrics.name: Revenue at risk from reset
keyMetrics.formula: anchor share x fee cut = 85% x 25% ≈ 21% of revenue

commonMistakes: Treating the 76% margin and 20-year contract as safe without reading the reset clause, which removes about ₹300 crore of EBITDA in two years.
Accepting the seller's 1.6x tenancy instead of testing it against the 1.08x to 1.15x trend and the largest operators' self-build behaviour.

frameworkPick.why: A financial investor must underwrite a standalone return and exit, and the return depends on whether tenancy growth can offset the anchor fee reset.

distractorWhyNot.ma: A financial buyer has no operating synergies to value; the test is standalone returns and exit, not combination value.
distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: Sizing backhaul demand is one input, but the question is whether to invest at this price and structure.

cases.title: Responding to a low-cost entrant we host
cases.prompt: Our client is the second-largest mobile operator in a Southern European country, with 30% share and an average postpaid price of €18 a month. A new low-cost entrant launched unlimited plans at €10 and has taken 4 points of share in a year, half of it from our client. Awkwardly, the entrant runs partly on our client's network under a wholesale deal worth about €90 million a year. How should the client respond? (All figures are illustrative case facts.)
clarifyingFacts: Q: How big is the damage? A: Assume the market has about 40 million postpaid lines. The entrant has 1.6 million; about 0.8 million came from the client, worth roughly €170 million of annual revenue.
Q: Who is switching? A: Mostly under-35s on SIM-only plans. Assume customers with fibre-plus-mobile or family plans churn at about half the rate of SIM-only customers and rarely move to the entrant.

Q: What is the wholesale deal? A: The entrant pays per GB, so the client's income grows as the entrant grows. The contract runs four more years, but the entrant is building its own network in the five largest cities and will move most of that traffic off within 2-3 years.

Q: What are others doing, and what does the board want? A: The market leader has launched a fighter brand at €12. The board wants to protect three-year EBITDA; the retail head wants to fight on price, while the wholesale head wants to keep the entrant growing on the client's network.

modelTree.label: How to respond to a €10 entrant we host, protecting three-year EBITDA?

children.label: How big is the threat to us?
Bundled and family customers: half the churn
How far the entrant can go
Entrant's likely share path over three years
Own network in five cities lowers its costs
How do we defend retail EBITDA?
Base-wide cut: reprices all 12 million lines
Move SIM-only users into fibre and family bundles
Targeted retention offers to at-risk users
How do we manage wholesale EBITDA from the entrant?
Value of hosting: €90m a year, falling as it self-builds
Longer, cheaper deal to delay its self-build
Hold terms and plan for lost city traffic
How will the rest of the market react?

hypotheses: A base-wide €2 cut would cost about €290 million a year across 12 million lines, more than the roughly €170 million at risk, so any price response must be targeted.
Wholesale income is temporary: once the entrant moves city traffic to its own network in 2-3 years, much of the €90 million goes, so protecting it should not stop the client defending retail.
Bundled and family customers churn at half the rate, so moving at-risk SIM-only users into bundles protects more EBITDA than matching €10.
hints: Split by the channels through which the entrant affects the client's EBITDA, not just by response options.
Branches: size of the threat, defend retail EBITDA, manage wholesale EBITDA, other players' reactions.
Defend retail: price moves (base-wide cut vs own second brand) and non-price moves (bundles, targeted retention).

keyMetrics.name: Annual revenue lost to entrant
keyMetrics.formula: lines lost x ARPU x 12 = 0.8m x €18 x 12 ≈ €173m

keyMetrics.name: Cost of a base-wide price cut
keyMetrics.formula: price cut x lines x 12 (€2 x 12m x 12 ≈ €288m)

keyMetrics.name: Net EBITDA effect of a response
keyMetrics.formula: retail EBITDA protected + change in wholesale EBITDA - cost of the response

commonMistakes: Matching €10 across the base, which reprices 12 million loyal lines to defend 0.8 million price-sensitive ones.
Treating wholesale and retail as separate decisions, when a second brand that wins back SIM-only users also cuts the entrant's traffic and the client's wholesale income.

frameworkPick.why: A rival's move triggers the question, and the main choices are about price (base-wide cut, second brand), weighed against wholesale income from the same rival.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: The cause of the EBITDA pressure is known; the question is how to respond, not why profit fell.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Knowing that SIM-only under-35s are leaving shapes the response, but the question is how to respond to a rival, not which customers to target.

quick.question: Which split of 'Revenue of an integrated Indian telecom operator' is MECE?
quick.parent: Revenue of an integrated Indian telecom operator

options.why: Gap: wholesale income beyond interconnect is missing, such as MVNO capacity, inbound roaming and tower or fibre leasing.
Mixed basis: products sit beside customer types, so an enterprise's mobile and broadband lines fall into two buckets.
One consistent basis (customer and product), every rupee in exactly one bucket, and 'wholesale and other' closes the list.
Overlap: IoT connections are sold to enterprises or consumers, so their revenue already sits in one of the first three buckets.

quick.question: Which split of 'A telecom circle's mobile subscribers at year end' is MECE?
quick.parent: A telecom circle's mobile subscribers at year end

options.why: Gap: misses deactivation of inactive and non-paying SIMs, which in Indian prepaid usually outnumbers port-outs.
Overlap: port-ins are new connections on our network, so they are already counted in gross additions.
Mixed basis: a stock split by plan type sits beside a flow, and this year's joiners are also prepaid or postpaid.
A complete stock-and-flow bridge: opening plus additions (including port-ins) minus all losses equals closing.

quick.question: Which split of 'Annual operating cost of one mobile tower site' is MECE?
quick.parent: Annual operating cost of one mobile tower site

options.why: Covers every operating cost pool of a site, and each cost belongs to exactly one bucket.
Overlap: generator running costs are fuel (already energy) and servicing (already maintenance).
Gap: misses diesel and battery backup energy, which at poor-grid sites can cost more than grid power.
Not a driver: buying radios is capex, not an annual operating cost of running the site.

quick.question: Which split of 'Mobile data traffic carried by an operator's network (GB per month)' is MECE?

options.why: Overlap: short-video apps are both video and social media, so their traffic fits two buckets.
Every connection is exactly one device type, and the split isolates fixed wireless homes, each using roughly ten times a phone's data.
Gap: misses fixed wireless home units, a fast-growing share of traffic once 5G home broadband launches.
Not a driver: revenue per GB is calculated from traffic and changes money earned, not the GB carried.

Revenue from additional tenants (rent, loading, energy)
options.why: Overlap: loading charges are already included in the revenue from anchor and additional tenants, so they are counted twice.

split: Energy margin (energy revenue minus energy cost)
options.why: EBITDA = rent and loading + energy margin - site costs - overheads, with each item counted once.
Not a driver: depreciation sits below EBITDA, so it does not change EBITDA.

quick.question: Which split of 'Prepaid ARPU (revenue per user per month)' is MECE?
quick.parent: Prepaid ARPU (revenue per user per month)

split: Share of users on each pack
Add-on and top-up spend per user
options.why: ARPU = sum of (pack share x monthly-equivalent price) + add-on spend, which covers every rupee a user pays each month.

split: Share of users on each pack
Add-on and top-up spend per user
options.why: Overlap: data boosters are add-on packs, already inside add-on and top-up spend.

split: Share of users on each pack
Add-on and top-up spend per user
options.why: Mixed basis: an 84-day pack's headline price covers three months, so mix x headline price does not give a monthly figure.

split: Share of users on each pack
Add-on and top-up spend per user
options.why: Not a driver: licence fee and spectrum charges are costs paid out of revenue, not part of what the user pays.

quick.question: Which split of 'Change in an operator's annual EBITDA after a 15% tariff hike' is MECE?
quick.parent: Change in an operator's annual EBITDA after a 15% tariff hike

split: Revenue lost to churn and downtrading
Change in other costs (retention offers, care)
options.why: Gap: misses revenue-linked costs; the licence fee, spectrum charges and commissions rise automatically with revenue.

split: Revenue lost to churn and downtrading
Change in Digital Bharat Nidhi contribution
options.why: Overlap: the Digital Bharat Nidhi contribution is 5 of the 8 points of the licence fee, already a revenue-linked cost.

split: Revenue lost to churn and downtrading
Rivals matching or not matching the hike
options.why: Mixed levels: rivals' choices are a cause of churn and downtrading, not a separate component of the EBITDA change.

split: Revenue lost to churn and downtrading
Change in other costs (retention offers, care)
options.why: Splits the EBITDA change into revenue and cost effects, with revenue-linked costs (licence fee, spectrum charges, commissions) shown separately because they move with the hike.

quick.question: Which split of 'Lifetime value of a 5G fixed wireless customer' is MECE?
quick.parent: Lifetime value of a 5G fixed wireless customer

options.why: Gap: the only cost is the upfront device; monthly levies, care and network cost are missing, so lifetime value is overstated.
LTV = monthly contribution x expected life - upfront cost (ignoring discounting), with each element counted once.
Overlap: backhaul is a network cost already deducted in monthly contribution.
Not a driver: payback is a result calculated from contribution and upfront cost, not a separate input to value.

chainDrills.prompt: Care call volumes jumped after a new pack launched with confusing validity terms. Which stage caused the problem?
chainDrills.why: The calls land in customer care (s6), but the cause is how the pack was designed and described, a product and pricing (s4) issue; extra care staff would treat the symptom.

chainDrills.prompt: Rural churn rose and exit surveys cite calls dropping during evening power cuts. Which stage holds the root cause?
chainDrills.why: The churn shows up in retention (s6) and looks like a network fault (s3), but sites going down when the grid fails is a site power backup problem, which sits in passive infrastructure (s2).

chainDrills.prompt: ARPU fell, and finance blames the care team's retention discounts. The data shows most of the fall came from customers moving on their own from 28-day to 84-day packs that cost less per month. Where did the problem start?
chainDrills.why: The retention discounts are a red herring: the fall comes from how the packs are priced against each other, as the long-validity pack gives a lower monthly-equivalent price. That is a product and pricing (s4) issue, not care (s6).

chainDrills.prompt: Put the stages of the mobile telecom value chain in flow order, from inputs to the end customer.
chainDrills.why: An operator first needs spectrum and licences, then passive infrastructure (towers, fibre, power) to host its active network. With a working network it designs products and prices, sells them through distribution, and finally bills, serves and retains the customer.

chainDrills.prompt: After a 20% tariff hike, revenue rose ₹1,000 crore, but costs rose ₹80 crore with no change in traffic, retailer payouts or headcount. Which stage does that cost increase sit in?
chainDrills.why: ₹80 crore is 8% of the extra revenue, which is the licence fee on adjusted gross revenue, a spectrum and licences (s1) cost. The hike happened in s4, and retailer payouts (s5) are ruled out by the prompt.

chainDrills.prompt: Assign each cost to the value chain stage it belongs to: diesel for the generator at a shared tower site; software licence fees for the 5G core network; fees paid to a streaming service bundled into postpaid plans; KYC verification cost for each new SIM; bad debt on unpaid postpaid bills; interest on deferred spectrum instalments.

items.item: Diesel for the generator at a shared tower site
Software licence fees for the 5G core network
Fees paid to a streaming service bundled into postpaid plans
KYC verification cost for each new SIM
Bad debt on unpaid postpaid bills

chainDrills.why: Diesel looks like a network running cost (s3), but at a shared site the tower company supplies power as part of passive infrastructure (s2) and passes it on to tenants. Streaming fees buy content to make plans more attractive, so they are a product cost (s4), not a distribution cost. Bad debt sits with billing and collections (s6). Interest on spectrum instalments is the financing cost of spectrum (s1), not network capex.
